formula.title: Guide for Conducting Risk Assessments: risk as a combination of likelihood and impact

bands.title: Risk appetite and risk tolerance statements are established, communicated, and maintained

bands.name: Very Low
bands.justification: Minimal exposure. Standard re-review every 2 years.

bands.name: Low
bands.justification: Acceptable with normal oversight. Annual re-review.

bands.name: Moderate
bands.justification: Original policy default: avoid. Change to 'Approved with Conditions' if your policy allows managed moderate risk.

bands.name: High
bands.justification: Avoid. Use only with formal leadership risk acceptance; re-review twice a year if accepted.

bands.name: Critical
bands.justification: Avoid. Use only with formal leadership risk acceptance.

factors.question: Does the vendor have a current independent security audit or certification that covers this product, such as SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, or one that fits our data (HIPAA, PCI DSS, FedRAMP, HITRUST)?

options.label: Yes
options.hint: A current SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001 or a framework that fits our data covers this product

options.label: No
options.hint: None found for this product (or only a logo, a Type I report or a report over 12 months old)

factors.justification: An independent audit (SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001) is the cheapest evidence that a vendor's baseline controls exist and were tested over time, which is why NIST CSF asks you to assess suppliers before you buy. Its absence adds 1 point, not 2, because a certificate shows controls exist, not that they stop breaches. A Type II report matters more than a logo: it covers how controls performed over months, not a single day.
factors.guidance: Look on the vendor's trust center, and ask for the report itself. A logo or badge alone doesn't count, and neither does a SOC 2 Type I report (it covers a single day) or one more than 12 months old. Check that it covers this product and plan. A framework that fits your data (HIPAA, PCI DSS, FedRAMP) also counts: each means a base level of controls exists and someone checks them.

references.title: Critical suppliers are assessed prior to acquisition
Planning and due diligence are performed to reduce risks before entering into supplier relationships
Software Acquisition Guide for Government Enterprise Consumers

factors.lookWhere: the vendor's trust center or security page; a SOC 2 or ISO certificate, or the report itself on request; ISO certificate lookups (IAF CertSearch); the FedRAMP Marketplace; HITRUST and PCI registries; trust pages hosted on Vanta, Drata or SafeBase

factors.question: Has the vendor had a data breach or serious security incident in the last 3 years?

options.label: Yes
options.hint: A breach or serious security incident hit the vendor (or its parent) in the last 3 years

options.label: No
options.hint: None found after checking at least two kinds of source (for example regulator or breach-notification records, and news)

options.label: Unknown
options.hint: Couldn't establish it either way (thin or conflicting sources, or sources that couldn't be reached)

factors.justification: A vendor that has already lost data once has shown how its controls fail and how it behaves under pressure: how fast it notified customers, how honest it was, what it fixed. Past breaches are the strongest single predictor available of future incidents, so this carries double weight. Note whether it was the vendor or a parent company, since the parent's practices can apply to you.
factors.guidance: Search the vendor's name with "breach", "incident" and "disclosure". Count incidents the vendor confirmed, or that regulators or established news outlets reported. Note whether it hit the vendor itself or its parent company. How they handled it is the next question.

references.title: Planning and due diligence are performed to reduce risks before entering into supplier relationships
Supplier risks are understood, assessed, responded to, and monitored over the course of the relationship

factors.lookWhere: the vendor's own incident notices, status page and security blog; state attorney-general breach notification listings (California, Maine, Texas and others); the HHS OCR breach portal; SEC 8-K cybersecurity filings (Item 1.05); Have I Been Pwned's breach list; established news

factors.question: Has the vendor been sued, fined, or reported on for questionable privacy practices in the last 3 years?

options.label: Yes
options.hint: A lawsuit, fine or regulator action over privacy practices, or credible reporting of them, in the last 3 years

options.label: No
options.hint: None found after checking at least two kinds of source (for example regulator or court records, and news)

options.label: Unknown
options.hint: Couldn't establish it either way

factors.justification: Regulatory actions, fines and lawsuits show how a vendor treats data when no one is watching. A pattern of privacy enforcement means the vendor's stated practices and real practices have diverged before, and may again. Double weight, same as breaches.
factors.guidance: Search regulator sites (FTC, state attorneys general, EU data-protection authorities) and established news outlets for lawsuits, fines, settlements and enforcement actions over privacy. Write down where you found it.

references.title: Planning and due diligence are performed to reduce risks before entering into supplier relationships
Supplier risks are understood, assessed, responded to, and monitored over the course of the relationship

factors.lookWhere: FTC cases and press releases; state attorney-general announcements; EU and UK data-protection authority decisions (Irish DPC, CNIL, ICO, noyb); court dockets (CourtListener, PACER) and class-action trackers; established news

factors.question: Is the vendor both small and new: fewer than 200 employees and in business fewer than 5 years?

options.label: Yes
options.hint: Both: fewer than 200 employees and in business under 5 years

options.label: No
options.hint: 200 or more employees, or in business 5 years or more

options.label: Unknown
options.hint: Couldn't find the headcount or founding date

factors.justification: Young, small vendors often lack a dedicated security team, and are more likely to fold, pivot or be acquired, which can change who holds your data. It carries a single point because size alone is not a flaw. NIST asks for supplier due diligence (GV.SC-06) but doesn't say small vendors are riskier, so this is a judgment call. It adds one point, and you can ignore it if company size doesn't matter to you.
factors.guidance: Use the company's own headcount (LinkedIn, its About page or filings) and founding date. Judge the company that runs the product, including a parent that operates it.

references.title: Planning and due diligence are performed to reduce risks before entering into supplier relationships

factors.ignoreNote: Company size isn't a security flaw, and no standard says small or young vendors are riskier. If your organization is comfortable buying from startups, ignore it.
factors.lookWhere: LinkedIn, Crunchbase, PitchBook or company filings for employee count and founding year; the vendor's About page. Check two when they disagree

factors.question: Does the vendor say which AI model(s) or model provider(s) power the product?

options.label: Yes
options.hint: Names the model or provider, or the product has no AI features

options.label: No
options.hint: Doesn't say which model or provider powers its AI features

factors.justification: If you can't name the model behind an AI feature, you can't assess where your data goes, whether it trains the model, or how outputs behave. Undisclosed models also hide dependence on a third-party AI provider that never appears in your contract. Double weight for AI tools; answer Yes for non-AI software.
factors.guidance: A named model or provider, a model card, or an AI entry on the sub-processor list all count as saying. Details about training data are nice to have but aren't required. Answer Yes for software that has no AI features.

references.title: Approaches for mapping AI technology and legal risks of its components, including third-party data or software
Value Chain and Component Integration

factors.lookWhere: product documentation, AI or trust pages, model or system cards, the sub-processor list, the privacy policy, and the vendor's announcements

factors.factor: Bought outside IT and Legal review
factors.question: Is this being bought outside of IT and Legal review, for example on a company card, expensed, or through a free self-signup?

options.label: Yes
options.hint: Bought or signed up for outside IT, Legal and Procurement review (company card, expense, free signup)

options.label: No
options.hint: Went through IT, Legal or Procurement review

factors.justification: Purchases that skip IT, Legal or Procurement skip the contract terms (DPA, liability, deletion, breach notice) that limit the damage when something goes wrong, and nobody is positioned to monitor the vendor afterwards. Shadow purchases are where most unreviewed data exposure starts.
factors.guidance: Confirm with Procurement or the team requesting it.

references.title: Requirements to address cybersecurity risks in supply chains are integrated into contracts
Planning and due diligence are performed to reduce risks before entering into supplier relationships

factors.question: What security rating does an outside rating service (UpGuard, SecurityScorecard, BitSight, Mozilla Observatory, Netskope CCI) give this vendor? Convert it to a 0 to 100 scale.
factors.justification: An outside-in rating gives you an independent, repeatable view of a vendor's internet-facing hygiene without needing its cooperation. NIST asks you to monitor supplier risk (GV.SC-07); which rating service you use is your choice. The band cut-offs are a convention, not a standard. 'Not rated' scores 2: unknown is treated as below average, not worst case.
factors.guidance: Pick the band for the score. Convert other scales first: letter grades A = 76-100, B = 51-75, C = 26-50, D or F = 0-25; UpGuard (0-950): divide by 9.5; BitSight (250-900): subtract 250, then divide by 6.5. If services disagree, use the lowest. Choose Not rated if no service has scored them.

references.title: Supplier risks are understood, assessed, responded to, and monitored over the course of the relationship

factors.lookWhere: the public pages for the vendor's domain on UpGuard, SecurityScorecard, BitSight, Mozilla Observatory and Netskope CCI; note the date of the rating

factors.question: Has the vendor been bought, merged, or changed owners in the last 12 months, or is a deal pending?

options.label: Yes
options.hint: Ownership changed in the last 12 months, or a sale or merger is pending

options.label: No
options.hint: No ownership change or pending deal found in press releases and company or filing records

options.label: Unknown
options.hint: Couldn't establish it either way

factors.justification: New owners often rewrite privacy terms, data-sharing and model choices after you've signed, and the acquirer's security and breach record starts to apply to your data. Contracts usually allow the vendor to assign them, so you may have no say. Worth a fresh look whenever ownership changes.
factors.guidance: Check press releases and the vendor's About page.

references.title: Supplier risks are understood, assessed, responded to, and monitored over the course of the relationship

factors.lookWhere: press releases and news; Crunchbase and PitchBook; SEC filings (8-K, S-4) for public companies; the vendor's About and investor pages

factors.factor: Our data goes to other AI companies
factors.question: Does the product pass our data to other companies' AI models or other third-party services (sub-processors)?

options.label: Yes
options.hint: Our data goes to named third parties, such as the AI model provider behind the product

options.label: No
options.hint: The vendor states in writing that our data isn't shared with third parties

options.label: Unknown
options.hint: No sub-processor list or statement could be found

factors.justification: Every sub-processor is another company that can leak, retain or train on your data, usually under terms you never negotiated. For AI tools this includes the model provider behind the product. Unknown scores the same as Yes because you can't assess a chain you can't see.
factors.guidance: Read the vendor's sub-processor list. A product built on another company's AI model almost always answers Yes. Choose Unknown if you can't find a list or a statement.

references.title: Policies and procedures address AI risks associated with third-party entities
Supplier risks are understood, assessed, responded to, and monitored over the course of the relationship

factors.lookWhere: the sub-processor list, DPA, privacy policy and trust center; the vendor's AI documentation

factors.question: Does a person approve every action the software takes, such as running code, sending messages, changing records, or making purchases?

options.label: Yes
options.hint: A person approves every action, or the software has no automation features

options.label: No
options.hint: It can act on its own (run code, send messages, change records, make purchases) without a person approving each action

options.label: Unknown
options.hint: The documentation doesn't say whether it can act without approval

factors.justification: Agentic tools turn a bad output into a bad action: sending email, changing records, running code. Prompt injection or a plain model mistake then has real consequences before a person can intervene. OWASP lists excessive agency as a top LLM risk. Double weight; answer Yes only if a person approves every action.
factors.guidance: Answer Yes only if a person has to approve every action, or the software has no automation features.

references.title: Excessive Agency
Human-AI Configuration

factors.lookWhere: product documentation and release notes (agents, automations, integrations, API actions); admin settings

factors.question: Does the plan we're buying offer single sign-on (SAML or OIDC) and a way for us to require multi-factor authentication?

options.label: Yes
options.hint: SAML or OIDC SSO is available on this plan and we can require MFA (through it or in the product)

options.label: No
options.hint: SSO isn't on this plan, we can't require MFA, or the documentation doesn't say

factors.justification: Without SSO and MFA, offboarding is manual, so ex-employees keep access, and one phished or reused password is enough to get in. Many vendors reserve SSO for enterprise tiers, so check the plan you are actually buying, not the plan on the marketing page.
factors.guidance: Check the plan you are actually buying, on the vendor's pricing page and admin documentation: SSO is often limited to enterprise tiers. If the documentation doesn't say, answer No and ask the vendor.

references.title: Identities and credentials for authorized users, services, and hardware are managed
Users, services, and hardware are authenticated
Ask whether SSO, MFA and logging come standard at no extra cost

factors.lookWhere: the pricing page and plan-comparison table for the specific plan; admin and SSO documentation; sso.tax

factors.question: Does the vendor's contract or terms promise in writing to delete our data on request and when the contract ends?

options.label: Yes
options.hint: The DPA or terms promise deletion on request and at the end of the contract

options.label: No
options.hint: No written deletion promise found (including when the DPA isn't public)

factors.justification: Data a vendor can't or won't delete stays exposed to every future breach, subpoena and acquisition, long after you stop using the product. A deletion clause with a timeframe, and ideally a certificate of destruction, is what makes offboarding a real exit.
factors.guidance: Look in the DPA or terms for a deletion clause with a timeframe. If the DPA isn't public, answer No and ask the vendor for it.

references.title: Plans include provisions for activities after the conclusion of a partnership or service agreement
Guidelines for Media Sanitization

factors.lookWhere: the DPA, terms of service and privacy policy; the trust center; data-deletion and retention help pages

factors.question: If the vendor has had a breach, did it handle it badly: downplay it, delay telling customers, or mislead people about it?

options.label: Yes
options.hint: It delayed notice, played the breach down or misled people

options.label: No
options.hint: It had a breach and handled it openly and promptly

options.label: No breach on record
options.hint: Nothing to judge, because the breach question above is No

options.label: Unknown
options.hint: Couldn't establish how the vendor handled it

factors.justification: Every company that suffers a breach learns something, and that's fine. What matters is how they behave. Vendors that delay notice, play it down, or mislead customers have shown that you would learn about the next incident late and incompletely, which is exactly when you need accurate facts. Adds 2 points on top of the breach question, so a vendor that both had a breach and covered it up scores noticeably worse than one that was open about it. Answer 'No breach on record' if there's nothing to judge, or Unknown if you can't tell how it was handled.
factors.guidance: Compare the vendor's own statements with what regulators and journalists later found. Was notice prompt? Did the first announcement understate what was taken? Learning from a breach and being honest about it should not count against a vendor. Hiding or minimizing it should. Answer "No breach on record" if the breach question above is No. Answer Unknown if there was a breach but you couldn't establish how it was handled.

references.title: Internal and external stakeholders are notified of incidents
The risks posed by a supplier are understood, recorded, prioritized, assessed, responded to, and monitored

factors.lookWhere: the vendor's breach notice compared with what regulators (state attorneys general, HHS, SEC, EU data-protection authorities) and journalists reported, and the timeline from discovery to notification

factors.question: Does the vendor's contract commit to telling us about a security incident within a set time, such as 72 hours?

options.label: Yes
options.hint: The contract commits to a specific time limit, in hours or days

options.label: No
options.hint: No specific time limit found: nothing at all, only "without undue delay", or the DPA isn't public

factors.justification: When something goes wrong, the clock starts for you too: you may have to notify customers, regulators or insurers within days. If the contract has no deadline for the vendor to tell you, you can learn about an incident weeks late. A commitment such as 72 hours is a common baseline. Contract terms like this are where NIST asks you to build security requirements into supplier agreements.
factors.guidance: Look for an incident or breach notification clause in the DPA or security addendum. Anything open-ended, like "without undue delay", with no number of hours or days counts as no deadline, so answer No. If the DPA isn't public, answer No and ask the vendor for it.

references.title: Cybersecurity supply chain requirements are established, prioritized, and integrated into contracts
Relevant suppliers are included in incident planning, response, and recovery activities

factors.lookWhere: the DPA or security addendum, the terms, and the trust center

factors.question: Does the vendor have a public way to report security flaws (such as a security.txt file, a disclosure policy or a bug bounty) and a good record of fixing them?

options.label: Yes
options.hint: A public way to report flaws exists and no poor patching record was found

options.label: No
options.hint: No public way to report flaws found, or a clearly poor record of fixing them (for example repeated, slowly patched CISA KEV entries)

factors.justification: Every vendor ships security flaws. What separates good vendors from risky ones is whether they take reports, fix issues on a known schedule, and tell customers. A published disclosure policy and fix timelines are signs of that. Their track record counts too: a vendor whose products keep showing up in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list, or that took months to patch past critical flaws, is telling you how it will behave next time.
factors.guidance: Look for a security.txt file, a vulnerability disclosure or bug bounty page, and a security advisories page. Then check the track record: search the vendor in CISA's KEV catalog, and look at how quickly past critical flaws were patched and announced. Published fix timeframes are a good sign but aren't required. Answer No if there's no way to report flaws, or if the track record is clearly poor.

references.title: Processes for receiving, analyzing, and responding to vulnerability disclosures are established
Questions buyers can ask vendors about vulnerability handling
Vulnerabilities actively exploited in the wild

factors.lookWhere: security.txt on the vendor's domain; its disclosure policy or HackerOne/Bugcrowd page; its security advisories (PSIRT) page; CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog; the NVD and CVE records, including CISA's enrichment (Vulnrichment, with SSVC decision points) to see how serious and exploited past flaws were; GitHub Security Advisories

factors.factor: What if it failed or the vendor vanished?
factors.question: If this software stopped working or the vendor went out of business, how bad would that be for us?
factors.justification: This is the business-continuity view of impact: if the tool fails, is breached or disappears, how badly do operations suffer? Tools with an easy fallback are low-impact however likely a failure is.
factors.guidance: Catastrophic = core operations stop, or it is a single point of failure with no workable alternative. Unacceptable = major disruption, but there are workarounds. Acceptable = easy fallback, such as another tool or a manual process.

references.title: Suppliers are known and prioritized by criticality
Assets are prioritized based on classification, criticality, resources, and impact on the mission

factors.question: Does it support critical teams or business processes, such as finance and payments, executive leadership, or core operations?

options.label: Yes
options.hint: It supports finance, leadership or core operations

options.label: No
options.hint: It's a convenience or supporting tool

factors.justification: Critical processes magnify any incident: an outage or breach in a tool that supports revenue, safety or compliance work hurts far more than the same event in a convenience tool. Weighted 3 (the maximum) by design. Edit the examples in the question to match your own critical functions.
factors.guidance: Edit the examples in this question to match your critical functions.

references.title: Suppliers are known and prioritized by criticality
Assets are prioritized based on classification, criticality, resources, and impact on the mission

factors.factor: Most sensitive data it will touch
factors.question: What is the most sensitive information this software will handle?
factors.justification: The harm from a breach grows with how sensitive the data is. This is the standard classification ladder (FIPS 199 style) used for deciding how much protection data needs. Answer for the most sensitive data that will realistically enter the tool, not the typical case, since that is what a breach would expose.
factors.guidance: Sensitive = personal data, financial or health records, credentials, source code with secrets. Confidential = non-public business information such as contracts, strategy or customer lists. Internal = everyday work content that would be little more than awkward if leaked. Public = already public. Pick the highest level that will realistically go into it, not the typical case.

references.title: Standards for Security Categorization of Federal Information and Information Systems
Assets are prioritized based on classification, criticality, resources, and impact on the mission

factors.question: If that information leaked, could it directly harm the people it describes (identity theft, safety, financial loss)?

options.label: Yes
options.hint: A leak could directly hurt the people the data describes

options.label: No
options.hint: A leak would cost or embarrass the company but not directly harm individuals

factors.justification: This separates exposures that are embarrassing from exposures that hurt real people: identity theft, physical safety, lost money or denied services. Harm to individuals brings legal duties, notification costs and reputational damage that no technical fix undoes.
factors.guidance: Think about the individuals behind the data, not the company.

references.title: PII confidentiality impact levels

factors.question: How widely will it be used at our organization?
factors.justification: Blast radius: the more users and teams rely on a tool, the more data it holds, the more accounts can be phished, and the harder it is to switch off or replace after something goes wrong.
factors.guidance: Use the planned rollout, not just the pilot.

references.title: Potential impacts and likelihoods of threats exploiting vulnerabilities are identified and recorded

factors.question: What is the most access it will have to our other systems?
factors.justification: Read-only access means a compromised vendor can see your data; write or admin access means it can change your systems, send messages as you, or pivot into other tools. OAuth scopes and API permissions show how far a compromise could reach.
factors.guidance: Admin or write access = it can change your data or settings, or act as your users. Read-only integration = it can only read. Standalone = nothing is connected to it. Look at the OAuth scopes and API permissions it asks for.

references.title: Access permissions incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties

factors.question: Will it handle data about children or other vulnerable people, such as patients or people in crisis?

options.label: Yes
options.hint: It will handle data about children or other vulnerable people

options.label: No
options.hint: It won't handle data about children or other vulnerable people

factors.justification: Data about children, patients or other vulnerable people carries a higher legal duty of care (for example COPPA, or GDPR Recital 38) and does more harm when exposed. Regulators treat these cases more severely, and people in them often can't protect themselves.
factors.guidance: Include data about students, patients, benefit recipients, and anyone who can't easily protect themselves.

references.title: Likelihood and magnitude of each identified impact are identified and documented
PII confidentiality impact levels
Children's Online Privacy Protection Rule

factors.question: Does the vendor's AI have effective safeguards against producing explicit, violent, deceptive, or degrading content?

options.label: Yes
options.hint: Effective safeguards exist (filters, usage policies, abuse monitoring), or the product has no AI

options.label: No
options.hint: The AI can produce such content and the vendor lacks real safeguards

factors.justification: A values check. A 'No' adds +0.5 to the preference multiplier, raising the whole score by 50%. It is a multiplier rather than points because values concerns should scale the risk, not sit beside it. NIST AI 600-1 names these as generative-AI risks, but there is no NIST guidance on how much they should count against a vendor, so weighing them is an organizational choice.
factors.guidance: Answer for the vendor's AI, including a parent company's models if they power this product. Answer Yes for software with no AI.

references.title: Dangerous, Violent, or Hateful Content
Obscene, Degrading, and/or Abusive Content

factors.lookWhere: safety and usage-policy pages, model or system cards, trust-and-safety documentation, independent evaluation or red-team reports, news

factors.factor: Consent and protections for vulnerable people
factors.question: Does the vendor get meaningful consent before training AI on personal data, and document its protections for children and people in crisis?

options.label: Yes
options.hint: Trains only with consent (or not on personal data), and protections are documented, or there's no AI

options.label: No
options.hint: Trains on personal data without meaningful consent, or has no documented protections for children and people in crisis

factors.justification: A values check (+0.5×). Using AI in ways that exploit or manipulate vulnerable people is a reputational and ethical risk beyond technical security. NIST AI 600-1 (Data Privacy) and AI RMF MAP 5.1 relate to it, but how heavily to weigh it is an organizational values choice.
factors.guidance: Read the privacy policy and any child-safety or crisis-response documentation. Answer Yes for software with no AI features.

references.title: Data Privacy
Likelihood and magnitude of each identified impact are identified and documented

factors.lookWhere: the privacy policy, data-processing terms, AI documentation, child-safety and crisis-response pages, regulator actions

factors.factor: Training on our data, vendor access
factors.question: Does the vendor commit not to train its AI on our data (or let us opt out), and not to read or review our content beyond narrow abuse and safety checks?

options.label: Yes
options.hint: No training on our data (or an opt-out we can use), and no routine access to our content

options.label: No
options.hint: Trains on our data with no opt-out, or reserves the right to read or review our content beyond narrow abuse and safety checks

factors.justification: A values check (+0.5×) about stewardship of data entrusted to you. Contract terms are covered by GV.SC-05, but treating vendor training on your data or staff access to your content as a concern that scales the whole score is an organization preference. Check the signed DPA, not marketing pages, since the two often differ.
factors.guidance: Check the signed DPA and terms, not marketing pages.

references.title: Data Privacy
Requirements to address cybersecurity risks in supply chains are integrated into contracts

factors.lookWhere: the signed DPA and terms (not marketing pages), the privacy policy, AI data-usage FAQs, and admin settings for training opt-outs

factors.question: Does the vendor store or process our data outside our country (or outside the regions our policies allow)?

options.label: Yes
options.hint: Our data, backups or support access sit outside the regions we allow

options.label: No
options.hint: Everything stays in the regions we allow

options.label: Unknown
options.hint: Couldn't establish where our data, backups or support access sit

factors.justification: A values and legal check (+0.5×). Where data is stored decides which governments and courts can demand it, and which privacy laws apply. Moving data across borders can break contractual or regulatory duties (for example GDPR transfer rules). Many organizations also simply don't want their data leaving their own country. Which regions are acceptable is your call, so edit the question to name them.
factors.guidance: Check the vendor's data-residency page, sub-processor list, and DPA for storage and support locations. Include backups and support staff who can view the data. Edit this question to name the countries or regions you require.

references.title: Cybersecurity supply chain requirements are established, prioritized, and integrated into contracts
Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management Practices for Systems and Organizations (covers supplier location, ownership and foreign influence)
General principle for transfers of personal data to third countries

factors.ignoreNote: NIST and CISA don't say data must stay in any particular country. Where data lives is your organization's rule, and it only matters if you have one: a law (such as GDPR transfer limits), a government or customer contract, or a promise to customers. If none of those apply, ignore it. Keep it if any do.
factors.lookWhere: data-residency and region pages, the sub-processor list with locations, the DPA and trust center

factors.question: Is the vendor, its parent company, or any place that stores, processes or supports our data in a country or region under U.S. OFAC sanctions (for example Iran, North Korea, Cuba, or the Crimea region)?

options.label: Yes
options.hint: The vendor, its parent, or a data center or support team is in a sanctioned country or region

options.label: No
options.hint: None of them are in a sanctioned place

options.label: Unknown
options.hint: Couldn't establish where the vendor, its parent, data centers or support teams are

factors.justification: A values and legal check (+0.5×). U.S. persons and companies generally can't do business with sanctioned countries or the people and companies in them, and violations carry serious penalties regardless of intent. A vendor, parent company, support team or data center in a sanctioned place brings that exposure to you. Check the current OFAC list, since sanctions change. Your legal team may want this to be an automatic denial: you can set a hard stop on this question in your policy.
factors.guidance: Check where the company is headquartered and owned, and where its data centers and engineering or support teams are. Sanctions change, so use the current OFAC list rather than examples. Ask Legal if unsure.

references.title: Planning and due diligence are performed to reduce risks before entering into supplier relationships
Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management Practices for Systems and Organizations (covers supplier location, ownership and foreign influence)
Sanctions programs and country information

factors.lookWhere: headquarters and ownership (Crunchbase, filings), data-center regions and sub-processor locations, each checked against OFAC's Sanctions List Search

factors.question: Does the vendor stand behind its AI's output with an IP (copyright) indemnity?

options.label: Yes
options.hint: The vendor offers an IP indemnity, or the product has no AI

options.label: No
options.hint: The AI can reproduce copyrighted work and the vendor won't indemnify us

factors.justification: A values and legal check (+0.5×). AI trained on copyrighted material can reproduce it in its output. If your staff use that output in public or product work, you can end up publishing someone else's content, with the legal and reputational risk that follows. A vendor that stands behind its output with an IP indemnity is taking on part of that risk. One that doesn't is leaving it all with you. NIST AI 600-1 names intellectual property as a generative-AI risk but doesn't say how much it should count, so weighing it is your choice.
factors.guidance: Look for an IP or copyright indemnity in the terms (several large AI vendors offer one for paid plans), plus any lawsuits over training data. Answer Yes for software with no AI features.

references.title: Intellectual Property
Copyright and Artificial Intelligence

factors.lookWhere: the terms of service (IP or copyright indemnity commitments), AI product pages, and trackers of lawsuits over training data

factors.question: Does the vendor (or its parent) sell products for government surveillance, military or intelligence use, or hand customer data to government agencies beyond what the law requires?

options.label: Yes
options.hint: It sells surveillance, military or intelligence products, or hands customer data to governments beyond what the law requires

options.label: No
options.hint: Neither applies

options.label: Unknown
options.hint: Couldn't establish it either way

factors.justification: A values check (+0.5×). Some organizations don't want their money or data supporting surveillance, military or intelligence work, or sitting with a company that readily gives customer data to governments. Others have no concern. There's no published standard, so this is your organization's values choice. Edit the question to match your own position.
factors.guidance: Check the vendor's transparency report, government-request policy, and public contracts. Edit this question to match what your organization actually objects to.

references.title: Planning and due diligence are performed to reduce risks before entering into supplier relationships
Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management Practices for Systems and Organizations (covers supplier location, ownership and foreign influence)

factors.ignoreNote: No standard or law makes this a security question, and many organizations have no position on it. If yours doesn't, ignore it.
factors.lookWhere: the vendor's transparency report, its government-request or law-enforcement policy, public contracts (USAspending, SAM.gov), news

factors.question: Would it be hard to leave this vendor, for example no bulk export of our data in a usable format, proprietary file formats, or fees and penalties for leaving?

options.label: Yes
options.hint: Leaving would be hard: no usable bulk export, proprietary formats, or exit fees

options.label: No
options.hint: Data can be exported in usable formats and leaving is easy

options.label: Unknown
options.hint: Couldn't find the export tools or exit terms

factors.justification: A values and business check (+0.5×). If leaving is hard, you're stuck with the vendor's price increases, outages and policy changes, and you can't easily walk away after an incident. NIST asks that supplier plans cover what happens after the relationship ends. How much lock-in your organization will accept is a business choice.
factors.guidance: Look for a data-export tool or API, supported formats, and exit or termination terms in the contract.

references.title: Supply chain risk management plans include provisions for activities after the end of a partnership or service agreement
Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management Practices for Systems and Organizations (covers supplier location, ownership and foreign influence)

factors.ignoreNote: Lock-in is a business tradeoff, not a security flaw. For a tool that is easy to replace or low-stakes, you can ignore it. Keep it for anything you'd struggle to move off of.
factors.lookWhere: data-export tools and API documentation, supported formats, the contract's termination and exit terms, and the pricing page (exit fees)

factors.question: Do we have a signed data processing agreement (DPA) that bans training on our data and requires deletion when the contract ends?

options.label: Yes
options.hint: A signed DPA bans training on our data and requires deletion at the end

options.label: No
options.hint: Not signed, or missing either term

factors.justification: Contract terms make vendor promises enforceable. A signed DPA with no-training and deletion commitments turns a marketing claim into an obligation you can hold the vendor to. Cuts the final score by 10%. Count it only if signed, not just offered.
factors.guidance: Answer Yes only if it's signed, not just offered.

factors.question: Is zero-data-retention or privacy mode switched on by an admin for all our users, so no one can turn it off?

options.label: Yes
options.hint: An admin has enforced it for everyone, so no one can turn it off

options.label: No
options.hint: Not available, optional, or not enforced

factors.justification: Zero-retention or privacy mode removes most of the training and retention exposure at its source: if the vendor never keeps the data, a later breach or policy change can't expose it. It must be enforced for the whole organization, not left as a per-user setting. Cuts the final score by 10%.
factors.guidance: Confirm in the admin console that it is enforced, not just available.

references.title: Requirements to address cybersecurity risks in supply chains are integrated into contracts
The confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data-at-rest are protected

factors.question: Will people sign in through SSO, with accounts created and removed automatically (SCIM) and limited to named users?

options.label: Yes
options.hint: SSO plus automatic account creation and removal (SCIM), limited to named users

options.label: No
options.hint: Anything less than that

factors.justification: SSO with automated provisioning means access follows your identity system, so offboarding is immediate and passwords aren't reused. That shrinks account-takeover and orphaned-account risk. Cuts the final score by 5%.
factors.guidance: Needs a plan tier that supports SCIM.

Access permissions incorporate the principles of least privilege and separation of duties

factors.factor: Sensitive data blocked by technical controls
factors.question: Is sensitive data kept out of the tool by a technical control, such as a DLP rule, a CASB policy, or restricted permissions?

options.label: Yes
options.hint: A technical control keeps sensitive data out

options.label: No
options.hint: Only a written rule, or nothing

factors.justification: Enforced technical limits (DLP rules, blocked connectors, restricted scopes) work even when people are rushed or unaware, unlike policy-only limits. Cuts the final score by 10%. A written 'please don't paste PII' rule does not count.
factors.guidance: A written 'please don't paste personal data' rule does not count.

factors.question: Is approval limited to a pilot with an end date and a scheduled re-review?

options.label: Yes
options.hint: Approval is a time-boxed pilot with an end date and a scheduled re-review

options.label: No
options.hint: Approval is open-ended, with no end date or review

factors.justification: A time-boxed pilot caps your exposure while evidence is gathered: a small group, limited data, a fixed end date and a decision point. Cuts the final score by 5%.
factors.guidance: Put the end date and the review owner in the notes.
